title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
Problem: Forecast two years of monthly turnover for Western Australia’s specialised food retailers (butchers, bakeries, fruit and vegetable shops).
Approach: A log transform and STL decomposition, then shortlists of ARIMA and ETS models compared on a 24-month holdout and checked against ABS data released later.
Result: On 2023-24, ETS(A,A,A) had a 2.7% average error (MAPE), against 4.7% for ARIMA, which fell below the actual value in 23 of 24 months.
Skills: R, fpp3 (fable, feasts, tsibble), Box-Cox transforms, STL, ARIMA, ETS, unit-root tests, residual diagnostics.

title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
The question
How accurately can you forecast a retail sector’s monthly turnover two years ahead, using nothing but its own history? And when two reasonable models disagree, which one should you trust? This was the main project for Monash’s ETC3550 Applied forecasting unit. It is judged here against data that was released after the forecasts were made.

title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
Data and cleaning
The series is ABS Retail Trade, Australia (8501.0), series A3349508C: monthly turnover for WA’s “other specialised food retailing” subgroup. That covers food retailers other than supermarkets and liquor stores. It runs from April 1982 to December 2022 (489 months), in current dollars and not seasonally adjusted.
The series is not a smooth curve. Average monthly turnover rose about ninefold, from $13M in 1983 to $122M in 2022. Most of that rise came in steps that line up with WA events, such as the 2012-13 peak of the mining boom and its 2016-17 slump. A robust STL decomposition flagged 11 unusual months, and I matched each one to a likely cause before modelling. Examples are Y2K stockpiling, the first month of the GST, an April-June 2010 jump that looks like an ABS sample change, and March 2020 panic buying.



Fig 1. Turnover grew in steps tied to WA events (shaded A-G), not along a smooth trend, so a model has to absorb sudden level shifts.

title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
Method, and why this one
Transformation. The seasonal swings grow with the level, so I took a log. Guerrero’s method suggested \(\lambda = -0.29\). That estimate was pulled around by the level shifts, while the log evened out the variance just as well and lets results be read as percentages.
Differencing. KPSS supported a seasonal difference alone. But annual growth drifted away from its average for years at a time, so I also took a first difference and kept a \(d = 0\) model as a check. That model did worse on the test set (6.3% against 5.0% MAPE).
Model choice. I picked ARIMA orders by hand from the ACF and PACF and used the automatic search only as a check. The hand-picked “airline” model, ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12, beat the automatic choice by about 89 AICc points. The search missed it because fable rules out a seasonal MA coefficient this close to -1. AICc can’t compare an ARIMA model with an ETS model, because they compute likelihoods differently, so the final choice between them was made on the holdout.

The refitted ETS model won because it learned faster growth from the last two years of data. That sensitivity is also its main risk.

title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
Findings
On the 2021-22 holdout, ETS(A,A,A) beat the ARIMA model on every accuracy measure (RMSE $5.9M against $6.5M, MAPE 4.5% against 5.0%). Both over-forecast 2021, because training ended just after the COVID-19 jump, when 2020 turnover averaged 19% above 2019.
I then refitted both models on all the data to December 2022. The ARIMA estimates barely moved. The ETS growth parameter rose from almost zero to 0.028, which lifted its forecast growth from about 5% to 7% a year. The ABS released 2023-24 data afterwards, so I could check both forecasts:



Fig 2. ETS tracked 2023-24 turnover closely because it adapted to recent growth, while ARIMA’s long-run growth rate left it below the actual value in 23 of 24 months.


Actual turnover averaged $132M a month in 2023 and $144M in 2024. ETS forecast $129M and $141M, a MAPE of 2.7% and a MASE of 0.60, so its errors were well below those of a seasonal naive forecast. ARIMA forecast $127M and $136M, with a MAPE of 4.7% and a MASE of 1.09. Its errors were systematic rather than random. Every actual value from both models fell inside its 80% interval, so the intervals were wider than they needed to be.

title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
What this means in practice
A two-year turnover forecast like this would support supplier contracts, staffing and stock planning for a food retailer or wholesaler. The project suggests a simple way to use it. Plan around the more adaptive model, but keep the conservative one as a floor scenario, since the two models only parted ways once recent growth dominated. Before relying on either, check whether the drivers of recent growth (population growth and food inflation) are expected to continue. Neither model can see them.

title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
Assumptions and limitations

Current dollars. The series isn’t adjusted for inflation, so part of the “growth” is price change. If inflation shifts, both forecasts go wrong in the same direction.
Univariate models. Both use only past turnover. They can’t anticipate shocks like the GST or COVID-19, or use drivers such as WA population growth.
The ETS win is partly luck. Its advantage came from a parameter that moved when two unusual years (post-COVID levels and food inflation) were added. Had growth slowed in 2023-24, ARIMA would probably have done better.
A short, distorted holdout. Model selection rested on 24 test months that started just after the COVID-19 jump.
Prediction intervals. The residuals have long tails (kurtosis about 9, against 3 for a normal distribution). That inflates the estimated variance, so the intervals were too wide for ordinary months and say little about rare shocks.
Residual checks. The ARIMA residuals pass the Ljung-Box test (p = 0.31). The ETS residuals only just pass (p = 0.058) and show some lag-1 autocorrelation it doesn’t model.
No more updates. The ABS stopped this publication after June 2025, so the forecasts can’t be checked beyond that.

None of this supports claims about why turnover grew. The models describe patterns in the series. They don’t explain them.

title: Can a two-year forecast keep up with WA food spending?
text:
The full report
The complete report covers 11 sections: exploration, the transformation and STL choices, unit-root tests, every candidate model, residual diagnostics, the forecasts and the ABS check. All the R code is in folded blocks. The data loads from the public Monash retail dataset and the ABS website, so the report runs from scratch.

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
Problem: Can unsupervised methods work out whether a news article is about sport, film or politics from its word frequencies alone?
Approach: Hierarchical clustering on cosine distance, plus document and term co-occurrence networks, on a hand-built corpus of 20 articles.
Result: 12 of 20 genre labels recovered (60%, against a 33% chance baseline). The main cause of errors was a preprocessing setting, not the clustering.
Skills: R, tm, igraph, text preprocessing, clustering, network analysis, hypothesis testing.

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
The question
Given only the words a news article uses - no author, no section, no tags - can you work out what kind of article it is? I built a corpus of 20 articles across three genres (sport, film, politics) and tested whether unsupervised methods could recover those genre labels from term frequencies alone. The labels were held back and used only to score the result.

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
Data and cleaning
The corpus is 20 news articles published between November 2024 and June 2025, drawn from the BBC, the Guardian, ABC News, news.com.au, ESPN, Variety, Time Out and The Conversation. Each was saved as a plain text file named for its subject, giving a roughly even split: 7 sport, 6 film, 7 politics.
Preprocessing followed the standard tm pipeline - strip numbers and punctuation, lowercase, drop English stopwords, collapse whitespace, then stem with Snowball. Three tokens survived and had to be removed by hand: the en dash, the opening curly quote, and the possessive 's. All three are non-ASCII, so removePunctuation never touched them - a reminder that a textbook pipeline will not match real scraped text without inspection.
The document term matrix was then trimmed with removeSparseTerms(sparse = 0.7), leaving 20 documents by 28 terms. That threshold is aggressive: it keeps only terms appearing in at least 30% of documents, which makes the matrix small enough to visualise but also, as it turns out, strips most of the genre-specific vocabulary.
View the code on GitHub

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
Method, and why this one
Hierarchical clustering on cosine distance, with Ward linkage. Cosine rather than Euclidean because these documents differ substantially in length - the film reviews run to nearly 500 words while several sport pieces are under 150. On raw counts, Euclidean distance would read that length gap as topical difference and cluster long documents with long documents. Cosine normalises it away by comparing direction rather than magnitude.
I then cut the tree at k=3 to match the three known genres, and separately built two co-occurrence networks from the binary document-term matrix: one linking documents that share terms, one linking terms that share documents. Eigenvector centrality on each identified the structurally important nodes.

Clustering gave a single hard label per document. The network showed that several documents genuinely sit between genres - which is the more honest description of what modern journalism looks like.

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
Findings
Clustering recovered the genre labels for 12 of 20 documents, or 60% accuracy against a 33% baseline. Better than chance, but a long way from reliable.



Fig 1. Cut at three clusters, the dendrogram recovers 12 of 20 labels - sport concentrates in one branch, while film and politics each split across two.


The errors are informative rather than random. The Brisbane Olympics article is labelled sport but landed in politics - it is largely about Queensland government funding. The Sydney FC piece is a sports story about a chairman appointment, and shares governance vocabulary with political reporting. Three political articles landed in the film cluster, all beside action films whose reviews borrow the language of conflict.
The document network makes the overlap visible in a way the dendrogram cannot.



Fig 2. Film articles occupy the centre of the document network - Mountainhead scores 1.00 on eigenvector centrality, Brexit_Weakening_Nature_Laws 0.96, Mission_Impossible 0.86.


Five of the six film articles rank among the most central documents - an artefact worth naming, since film reviews are the longest documents here and so carry more of the surviving high-frequency terms. Centrality is partly measuring length.
The token network explains the 60% ceiling directly.



Fig 3. The terms left after sparse-term removal are journalistic filler - last, one, will, new and time are the most central, and none of them carry genre.


Nothing there distinguishes a film review from an election report. The sparsity threshold kept the terms appearing everywhere, which is exactly the set that separates nothing - the clustering was working from vocabulary whose signal had already been filtered out.
Only the bipartite view shows genre structure cleanly, because it keeps the document-term attachments instead of collapsing them into one projection.



Fig 4. In the bipartite view, govern and hous attach to the politics documents - the genre signal survives only when documents and terms are shown together.


Sentiment analysis was a secondary check, and it found nothing. Across nine two-sided t-tests - overall sentiment, positivity and uncertainty, each across all three genre pairs - not one reached p < 0.05, before or after correction. Sport scores lowest on positivity descriptively, but at n = 20 that gap is not distinguishable from noise.



Fig 5. Sport sits lowest on positive sentiment, but no pairwise difference between genres reaches significance.


The tempting version of this result is available, which is worth being precise about. Test one-sided in the direction the boxplots already suggest and film beats sport on positivity at p = 0.037 - a hypothesis chosen after seeing the data, the only one of nine comparisons to clear the line, and it does not survive Bonferroni correction. Two-sided is the honest test here.

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
What this means in practice
The same pipeline is how you would start on unlabelled text in a business - customer feedback, support tickets, open-ended survey answers - to find themes before anyone has tagged them. The lesson that transfers is the sparsity threshold: the setting that made the networks readable also removed the vocabulary that mattered, so in practice I would tune it against a small hand-labelled sample before trusting the clusters. And documents that sit between groups are a finding, not an error - a ticket that is both a billing question and a complaint belongs in both queues, which a single hard cluster label cannot express.

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
Assumptions and limitations
The honest summary is that this shows the method working, not a result worth trusting.

n = 20 is far too small. With 6 to 7 documents per genre the t-tests have almost no power, which is the most likely reason none of them detect anything. A null result at this sample size is not evidence that the genres have similar sentiment - it is mostly evidence that the design cannot tell.
The corpus is not a random sample. I chose the articles myself, so my own sense of a typical sport or film piece is baked into both sample and labels.
Genre labels are my own judgement. Misclassifications concentrate in documents that genuinely span topics, so part of the 40% error is disagreement about the label rather than failure of the clustering.
k=3 was imposed, not discovered. I cut the tree at the number of genres I already knew, and did not check whether the dendrogram supports three clusters.
Centrality is confounded with document length, which I did not normalise for. That film articles are central is partly a finding that they are long.
sparse = 0.7 was tuned for legible networks, not for accuracy. It removed the genre-specific vocabulary the task needed, and is the most likely cause of the 60% ceiling. I did not test other thresholds.
Stemming is lossy and was not validated. Snowball produces hous, includ, govern; I did not check what it merged.

What this does not license: any claim about news genres in general, or that 60% is the achievable accuracy here. A larger corpus with a tuned sparsity threshold would almost certainly do better.

title: Can word frequencies alone tell sport from politics?
text:
Reproducing this
Written in R with tm, SnowballC, SentimentAnalysis, proxy and igraph, as four sequential scripts in the code repo.
The corpus is 20 copyrighted news articles and is not redistributed, but the derived document-term matrix is - so the clustering and all three network figures reproduce from the repo alone, with no corpus needed. SOURCES.md lists every article URL if you want to rebuild it and re-run the sentiment step. The layout seed is fixed, so the network figures come out identical.

title: ICU Mortality Probability Prediction
text:
Problem: Rank ICU patients by their risk of dying in hospital, using what is known when they arrive, so attention goes to the highest-risk patients first.
Approach: Five model families compared under one fixed preprocessing recipe, then a LightGBM and XGBoost blend tuned with repeated cross-validation.
Result: Out-of-fold ROC-AUC of 0.942; the top grade band started at 0.94. Logistic regression beat the neural network.
Skills: R, tidymodels, LightGBM, XGBoost, feature engineering, cross-validation.

title: ICU Mortality Probability Prediction
text:
The question
Given only what is known about a patient at the moment they arrive in intensive care, how well can we predict whether they will die before discharge? The purpose is triage rather than explanation - ranking patients so that limited clinical attention flows toward the people most likely to need it.
The work was a Kaggle competition for a machine learning unit, graded on ROC-AUC on a hidden test set in bands topping out at 0.94. Submissions had to be probabilities, so nothing could be tuned to a threshold, and the leaderboard only showed the score on half the test set - the mark came from the other half.

title: ICU Mortality Probability Prediction
text:
Data and cleaning
A preprocessed extract of MIMIC-III, one row per ICU stay: first-day vital signs summarised as min, max and mean, demographics and admission details, plus a separate table of ICD-9 diagnosis codes. The outcome, HOSPITAL_EXPIRE_FLAG, is positive for roughly 11.2% of stays.
Three parts needed care:
Age had to be reconstructed. MIMIC shifts the date of birth of any patient over 89 roughly 300 years into the past as a de-identification measure, so a naive ADMITTIME - DOB returns ages in the hundreds. Ages were capped at 90, with an indicator kept, because being old enough to be date-shifted is itself a signal.
The diagnosis columns were unusable raw. Free-text DIAGNOSIS held about 5,000 unique values and behaved as an ID column, so it was dropped. The 555 ICD-9 codes were rolled into the ~17 standard chapters, and for the boosting pass also multi-hot encoded over the 300 most common codes.
Derived features carried more signal than raw levels: per-vital ranges, shock index and pulse pressure. A heart rate of 110 means something different at a systolic pressure of 140 than at 80.


Code
fe_basic <- function(df) {
  df |>
    mutate(
      age_days    = as.numeric(difftime(ADMITTIME, DOB, units = "days")),
      AGE         = pmin(pmax(age_days / 365.25, 0), 90),
      AGE_OVER_89 = as.integer(age_days / 365.25 > 89),

      HeartRate_Range = HeartRate_Max - HeartRate_Min,
      SysBP_Range     = SysBP_Max     - SysBP_Min,

      ShockIndex    = HeartRate_Mean / na_if(SysBP_Mean, 0),
      PulsePressure = SysBP_Mean - DiasBP_Mean
    ) |>
    select(-DOB, -ADMITTIME, -Diff, -DIAGNOSIS, -age_days)
}


Encoding is the step most likely to fail silently. Levels are fitted on train and applied to test, so an unseen test level becomes NA instead of quietly shifting every column to its right:


Code
for (c in cat_cols) {
  lev <- unique(train_fe[[c]])
  # -1L because factor() codes from 1, while LightGBM wants categoricals from 0
  train_fe[[c]] <- as.integer(factor(train_fe[[c]], levels = lev)) - 1L
  test_fe[[c]]  <- as.integer(factor(test_fe[[c]],  levels = lev)) - 1L
}


View the code on GitHub

title: ICU Mortality Probability Prediction
text:
Method, and why this one
The project ran in two passes. The first held preprocessing fixed - rare-level consolidation, one-hot encoding, then standardisation - and swapped only the model. Five families were fitted this way: logistic regression, kNN at k = 25, a random forest, a 16-unit single-layer MLP, and XGBoost.
The second pass pushed gradient boosting further: richer diagnosis features, stratified cross-validation repeated over 3 seeds x 5 folds with early stopping, and a 70/30 blend of LightGBM and XGBoost. Repeating the folds matters at an 11% positive rate, where a single 5-fold split carries enough noise to move the estimated AUC on its own:


Code
for (seed in c(42L, 123L, 2024L)) {
  fold_idx <- make_folds(y, N_SPLITS, seed)   # stratified on the outcome
  seed_oof <- rep(0, length(y))

  for (k in seq_along(fold_idx)) {
    va <- fold_idx[[k]]
    tr <- setdiff(seq_along(y), va)

    dtr <- lgb.Dataset(X[tr, ], label = y[tr], categorical_feature = cat_cols)
    dva <- lgb.Dataset(X[va, ], label = y[va], categorical_feature = cat_cols,
                       reference = dtr)

    m <- lgb.train(c(lgb_params, list(seed = seed)), dtr, nrounds = 4000L,
                   valids = list(val = dva), early_stopping_rounds = 100L)

    seed_oof[va] <- predict(m, X[va, ])       # each row scored by a model
    test_lgb     <- test_lgb + predict(m, X_test)   # that never saw it
  }
  oof_lgb <- oof_lgb + seed_oof
}


The blend weight came from the centre of the flat region of the weight sweep rather than its peak, since picking the exact top of a noisy curve is a quiet form of overfitting the validation set.
Boosting rather than a linear model because clinical risk is threshold-like - an SpO2 below 88 is categorically bad - which trees represent natively. Two boosting libraries rather than one because LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise and XGBoost level-wise, so their errors are partly decorrelated and the average beats either alone.

Logistic regression beat the neural network. On tabular data of this size, model capacity is not free - the extra flexibility has to be paid for in data, and here it could not be afforded.

title: ICU Mortality Probability Prediction
text:
Findings



Fig 1. The boosting blend reached 0.942 out-of-fold and logistic regression (0.829) scored above the random forest (~0.81), but these scores come from different evaluations.


On the public leaderboard, kNN scored 0.761, the MLP 0.771 and logistic regression 0.829. Logistic regression finishing ahead of the neural network suggests mortality risk is broadly additive in these inputs, which is exactly the structure a linear model captures most efficiently. The kNN result is structural rather than a tuning failure: after one-hot encoding, distances concentrate, and a 25-patient neighbourhood contains under three deaths on average.
The random forest baseline reached ~0.81, but that figure was reported under cross-validation rather than the leaderboard, so its gap to logistic regression is not a clean ranking. The first-pass XGBoost has no reported score, so it is not shown.
The final blend reached 0.942 out-of-fold. That number is not directly comparable to the leaderboard scores above - it comes from a different evaluation scheme on a feature set several hundred columns wider, so much of the gap is features rather than algorithm.

title: ICU Mortality Probability Prediction
text:
What this means in practice
A model like this would support clinical judgement, not replace it: a hospital could use it to order a review list so the highest-risk new admissions are seen first. Two things would have to change before that. The diagnosis codes would need replacing with information available at admission (see below), and the probabilities would need calibrating, because a ward planning staffing needs to know whether a score of 0.3 really means a 30% risk. The cost of errors is also lopsided - missing a patient who deteriorates is far worse than reviewing one who did not - so the alert threshold should be set on that trade-off, not on AUC.

title: ICU Mortality Probability Prediction
text:
Assumptions and limitations
Folds were stratified on the outcome, not grouped by patient. Splitting happened at ICU-stay level. If a patient contributes more than one stay, their rows can land in different folds and the model can effectively memorise them, inflating the out-of-fold estimate. Patient-level splitting via group_vfold_cv() is the fix. I have not quantified how much repeat admission exists in this extract, so I do not know the size of the effect.
Diagnosis codes are not available at hour zero. ICD-9 codes are assigned over the stay and finalised at discharge, so using them to predict that stay’s outcome is defensible as a retrospective benchmark but would not transfer to real-time use.
Logistic regression assumes independent observations and linearity in the log-odds. The first is questionable for the same repeat-admission reason; the second was not formally checked.
The probabilities are ranked, not calibrated. Rebalancing the positive class distorts the output scale and averaging fifteen models compresses it toward the middle. PR-AUC was computed alongside ROC-AUC, which is the right instinct at an 11% base rate, but no calibration plot was produced.
None of this licenses a claim that any feature causes mortality, or that acting on the model would change an outcome. It supports one claim only: the ranking is informative.

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
Problem: Draft a stronger fantasy basketball roster than the usual “last season’s totals” cheat sheet, using only information available before the season.
Approach: Player projections with an aging curve, a draft engine that maximises the starting lineup, and a leakage-free backtest over 13 seasons.
Result: +14.6% starting-lineup points over the naive draft, winning all 13 held-out seasons.
Skills: Python, pandas, nba_api, pytest, Streamlit, simulation, backtesting.

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
The question
In a fantasy basketball snake draft, twelve managers take turns picking real NBA players, and each week a team scores points from its starters’ box scores. Most managers draft from a cheat sheet ranked by last season’s totals. I wanted to know whether a model could do measurably better, using only information available before the season - and how to prove it without fooling myself.

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
Data and cleaning
Sixteen seasons of per-game player logs (2010-11 to 2025-26, about 26,000 rows a season) from the NBA.com stats API via nba_api, plus team rosters for positions and player bios for age, cached to Parquet.
Absence is data, but only after a player arrives. A season a player missed entirely is a durability signal - without it, an early version drafted retired players. So missed seasons count as zero games, but only from each player’s first appearance, or sophomores are penalised for seasons before they joined the league.
Missing positions are counted, never dropped. 208 board players had no position in the roster data. They are scored against an overall baseline and the count is reported each run.
The schema is verified, not assumed. Column names come from a real pull and are checked on every load, so a silent API change fails loudly.
View the code on GitHub

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
Method, and why this one
The project was built in versions, each kept only if it beat the one below it:

Projection. Last season’s total, then a per-game rate times projected games played, an aging curve, and shrinkage toward a positional mean.
Board. Value over replacement, so a scarce centre outranks an equally good guard.
Draft engine. Only starters score, so a roster is worth its best legal starting lineup, not the sum of all 13 players. The engine picks whoever adds most to my lineup, plus a penalty for positions about to run dry before my next turn. A greedy draft wastes picks on depth it can never start.

The baseline is the naive “last season’s totals” draft, not a random one - beating random by 153% only shows the code is wired up. Every projection for season N uses only seasons before N, enforced by an assertion and a test that forces it to fail.

The first backtest gave every team the same board, so upgrading the board upgraded the whole league and my edge cancelled out. Holding the other eleven teams fixed is what made the effect measurable.

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
Findings
With the other eleven teams drafting naively and only my strategy changing, averaged over all twelve draft positions, the engine on the aging-curve board beat the naive draft by 14.6% in starting-lineup points. It won all 13 held-out seasons (2013-14 to 2025-26) and 85% of the 156 slot-seasons.



Fig 1. The draft engine is the only component that beats naive drafting on its own - and the better aging-curve board nearly doubles its edge, from +7.8% to +14.6%.


Drafting straight down the value-over-replacement board was 11.8% worse than naive: it inflated centres, so in 2023-24 it took Embiid and Vucevic while Doncic sat on the board. The better projection was worth nothing as a ranking on its own (-1.4%) but compounded through the engine.
Getting a number I trust took more work on the test than on the model:



Fig 2. Measured with every team on the same board, the engine shows no edge at all (-0.2%); holding the opponents fixed reveals a clear one (+7.8%).


Last season’s total proved a hard projection to beat. Only the aging curve improved it (mean absolute error 501.8 vs 508.9 points) and it cut the systematic over-prediction from +34.9 to +9.1 points per player. Shrinkage made every metric worse and was switched off.

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
What this means in practice
A better forecast was worth little until a decision rule used it properly. The same is true of ranking customers by predicted value: deciding who to target with a fixed budget has constraints, like the roster slots here, that a ranking ignores. The evaluation lesson transfers too - a comparison where the control group also changes, like every team drafting off the same board, can hide a real effect entirely.

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
Assumptions and limitations

Opponents are simple bots. The other eleven teams draft greedily and never react to my picks, so +14.6% is an upper bound, not a forecast.
The league settings are placeholders. Scoring and roster slots are a standard Yahoo-style setup until the Yahoo API connection is authorised.
Lineups are scored with hindsight by default. Re-scoring with lineups chosen from the projection instead gives +15.0%, so the conclusion does not depend on it.
Thirteen seasons is a small sample. After averaging the 12 draft slots, each season is one result, treated as independent. That separates +14.6% from zero (95% CI 9.0% to 20.3%) but does not pin down its size, and two COVID-shortened seasons add noise.
The aging curve has survivorship bias. It only sees players who lasted another season, so late-career decline is understated.
No rookies, no bench value. Players with no NBA history are absent, and in-season moves like streaming and trades are not modelled.

None of this licenses a claim that the tool wins leagues - the draft is only a modest lever. It shows a decision rule that reliably beats the cheat sheet most managers use.

title: Can a smarter strategy beat drafting off last season’s totals?
text:
Reproducing this
Python with pandas, nba_api, plotnine and pytest, plus a Streamlit app for draft day. The 72 tests run offline in seconds; a full backtest needs about 10 minutes of one-off API pulls. The code repo README lists every result table.

title: What predicts crime across Victoria’s LGAs?
text:
Problem: Find which demographic and economic factors explain differences in crime rates across Victoria’s 78 LGAs.
Approach: A 2011-2024 panel of 1,092 LGA-years, modelled with pooled OLS, fixed effects, factor analysis, LASSO and elastic net.
Result: Fertility and education go with lower crime, and unemployment and density with higher; elastic net predicted best (test R² 0.777).
Skills: R, panel econometrics, fixed effects, regularisation, choropleth mapping, data integration.

title: What predicts crime across Victoria’s LGAs?
text:
The question
Which demographic and economic factors explain the differences in crime rates across Victoria’s 78 local government areas (LGAs) between 2011 and 2024? This was a student research project for the Monash Statistical Analytics Club (MSAC), written with Sanjana Bhavin Lakhpatwala and Sayali Choudhary.

title: What predicts crime across Victoria’s LGAs?
text:
Data and cleaning
The panel covers 78 LGAs over 14 years (1,092 LGA-years). It joins Crime Statistics Agency Victoria offence data to ABS census data and other public indicators. Census variables only exist for 2011, 2016 and 2021, so each value was carried forward to the following years. A census-years-only regression gave the same signs and significance, which supports the fill. Unemployment is published by region, so each LGA was given its region’s rate.

title: What predicts crime across Victoria’s LGAs?
text:
Method, and why this one
The models build on each other: pooled OLS as a baseline, then LGA, time and combined fixed effects, then factor analysis, LASSO and elastic net to deal with strongly correlated predictors. The time fixed effects model removes shocks that hit every LGA in the same year. The combined model also removes anything constant about each LGA, so what remains is change within an LGA over time.

A variable can point one way when you compare LGAs with each other and the opposite way when you follow one LGA over time.

title: What predicts crime across Victoria’s LGAs?
text:
Findings
Fertility rate and education go with lower crime, and unemployment and population density with higher crime. Citizenship mix is significant across models, likely reflecting wider demographic and urban patterns rather than a direct effect.
Bachelor’s degree share shows why fixed effects matter. It is positive in the time fixed effects model, since inner Melbourne is both highly educated and high crime, but strongly negative within LGAs in the combined model (-245.5, p < 0.001).



Fig 1. Income, unemployment and certificate share are only significant for offence counts, which means their effect is mostly about population size.


Elastic net gave the best out-of-sample accuracy and was selected for prediction. The fixed effects models remain the better tool for explaining change within an LGA.

title: What predicts crime across Victoria’s LGAs?
text:
What this means in practice
The paper’s conclusion points policy toward education, employment and community stability as levers for reducing crime locally. The wider lesson carries over to any regional data: a pattern across areas, like educated councils having more crime, can reverse within each area over time. Before acting on a cross-area comparison, check whether the effect holds once each area is compared with itself.

title: What predicts crime across Victoria’s LGAs?
text:
Assumptions and limitations
As set out in the paper:

Education and citizenship are census-only and were carried forward, which assumes they change gradually.
Unemployment is assigned at regional rather than LGA level, which may add measurement error.
Models use different outcomes (crime rate vs offence count) and transformations, so RMSE and MAE are not directly comparable and model selection leans on MAPE.
Fixed effects cannot account for time-varying omitted variables such as policing intensity, policy changes or social programs.
LASSO and elastic net coefficients are biased by shrinkage and should be read as predictive, not causal.
Results are area-level associations, so applying them to individuals risks the ecological fallacy.
